transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-05 15:30 UTC | Duration: ~74 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood Infra SE); Amina (Equinox Head of ML), Lucas (Platform), Jenna (CTO), Samir (Security), Rae (NLP)

00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're here to walk through some of the options for your longform pipeline — I know you mentioned 128k plus tail contexts so Ethan's going to drive most of this.
00:18 Ethan Park: Hi all, short agenda: runtime patterns for append-heavy workloads, chunking approaches we recommend, KV cache and eviction — how we keep hot prefixes cheap — batching and per-request latency SLOs, then quantization and finally deployment modes (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private/VPC). Feel free to interrupt.
00:45 Amina Farouk: Great, thanks. Quick bit of context from our side: we produce multi-megabyte clinical narratives that we want to condition on in one shot for summarization and structured extraction. Typical request is append new notes and then ask multiple chained extractions. Our SLA: p95 generation latency under 3s for short responses but we're flexible for longer summaries — tail latency and cost are our main concerns.
01:12 Lucas Romero: For infra, we run on GCP with a private VPC. We're evaluating either Dedicated capacity on Redwood or a Private deployment in our VPC. We need to ensure no PHI leaves the VPC and have KMS in place.
01:35 Ethan Park: Makes sense. Two quick clarifications: when you say 128k+ context, is that 128k tokens active context per request or cumulative across chained calls?
01:48 Rae Martin: Mostly active context, we expect 128k tokens on initial conditionings, then appends of 1-2k tokens as new notes come in. So we need persistent KV-like behavior to avoid re-encoding the whole history.
02:05 Ethan Park: Good — that's exactly the use-case where prefix/KV caching reduces cost. Quick schematic: we keep the prefix KV in RAM/GPU memory and stream only the appended tokens through the attention for the last window, using a sparse or lazy attention for the earlier positions so they don't drive quadratic compute per step.
02:30 Samir Patel: On security, PHI means we must have client-owned keys before any tokenized data leaves, can you support HSM-backed KMS?
02:45 Priya Narang: Yes, Private deployments support customer KMS integration and HSM-backed key wrapping — we'll attach a doc. For Hosted we can do Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) with strict export controls but you mentioned you prefer isolated network, so Private is likely.
03:10 Jenna Park: Cost model question: what's the delta between keeping 128k in GPU memory vs sharded KV on NVMe with lazy fetch?
03:23 Ethan Park: Great question. If you keep the whole KV in GPU memory you get lowest latency — per-token compute for appended tokens is minimal because attention only walks the new tokens and KV lookups are local. But GPU memory cost rises linearly with KV size. With NVMe sharding and on-demand fetch there's an IO latency tax — we ship a hybrid: keep the hot window and sampled recent KV shards in GPU, cold shards on fast NVMe with prefetch heuristics. For many workloads we can get ~1.4–2x cost savings vs full-residency for large 128k+ stores at <15% tail-latency increase if the prefetch is tuned.
04:10 Amina Farouk: Can you expand on the prefetch heuristics? Our app tends to reference specific sections of the corpus more often (patient history).
04:22 Ethan Park: Prefetch is driven by request fingerprinting and RL-based heuristics in the runtime: we keep an LRU with frequency decay and predictive prefetch for keys referenced in recent queries. Also we do prefix compression — storing KV in compressed blocks and decompressing hot blocks into GPU. If your access pattern has locality, we hit high cache hit rates.
04:50 Lucas Romero: How often do you evict? Is it time-based or usage-based?
05:00 Ethan Park: Usage-based primarily. We maintain per-key hotness scores (access count, recency, predicted next-use). Eviction policy is frequency-decayed LRU with size-aware shrinking. There is also a background compaction that merges small KV blocks.
05:25 Rae Martin: For chunking, we normally split at paragraph/section boundaries. Any recommendations for chunk size and overlap for pharma docs? We don't want to lose cross-section dependencies.
05:40 Ethan Park: We recommend semantic-aware chunking where chunks are between 1k–4k tokens for 128k contexts, with a 128–512 token overlap window for cross-chunk attention. For structured extraction tasks we also add a per-chunk summary vector stored in the KV to give a cheap global signal. That plus a sparse global attention head keeps inter-chunk coherence.
06:12 Maya Chen: Quick interject — for the pilot we can show two variants: (A) GPU-resident KV for 128k but with expensive hardware footprint vs (B) hybrid NVMe prefetched KV with tuned prefetch that reduces cost. We'll run both against your dataset.
06:34 Jenna Park: What about quantization? We need to reduce model size but maintain accuracy on biomedical terms.
06:40 Ethan Park: We support per-layer mixed quantization profiles. For example, keep first N layers in FP16 or BF16, quantize the middle to 4-bit or INT8 with calibration on your domain data, and leave the final few layers higher precision. Our Optimize tooling suggests quant profiles per workload; for biomedical vocab we often observe minor headroom loss at 4-bit but can do 6-bit or mixed to preserve extraction fidelity.
07:05 Rae Martin: Do you ship the calibration scripts?
07:10 Maya Chen: Yes, we'll include calibration harness in the perf repo. You run on representative tokens and we produce a recommended quant map.
07:20 Samir Patel: If we do Private, how are audit logs surfaced? We need immutable logs for each inference and key access.
07:30 Priya Narang: Private mode includes an audit sink integration to your SIEM and immutable append-only logs saved to customer-managed storage. KMS audit events are forwarded to your audit log. We'll share a checklist doc.
07:52 Lucas Romero: Back to runtime: batching — how should we think about batching when requests are very long? Pooling multiple 128k requests seems impossible without exploding memory.
08:08 Ethan Park: Right, we avoid naive batching for ultra-long contexts. Our runtime does dynamic request slicing: it batches the prefix KV operations where possible and then executes the streaming/generation phase per request. Two patterns: micro-batching appended tokens across concurrent requests (if you have many small appends) and cross-request KV read batching for hot-key fetches. For initial conditioning with 128k tokens we typically treat it as a single shot per request; if concurrency is high we recommend dedicated capacity with larger GPU memory to keep multiple resident KVs.
08:50 Amina Farouk: Our concurrency is bursty — during nightly ingest we might have hundreds of appends. Will autoscaling handle that?
09:00 Maya Chen: Dedicated capacity supports autoscaling with burst nodes; we can define a policy to spin up warm nodes when queue depth crosses threshold. Private deployments also have autoscale controllers but constrained by your infra quotas.
09:15 Jenna Park: Are there recommended hardware types? We currently use A100s on GCP.
09:22 Ethan Park: A100 is solid. For 128k+ workloads bigger GPU memory is helpful; 80GB cards or multi-GPU pinned memory patterns are common. We also support systems with high-bandwidth NVMe for the hybrid KV pattern.
09:40 Lucas Romero: Any guidance on model architecture? We are evaluating a Llama-derivative and a sparse-attention-enabled model.
09:50 Ethan Park: Models with sparse-attention blocks or rerun-able chunked encoders are easier to scale. If the model supports block-sparse kernels we can shave compute on long-range attention. We also support kernel substitution to use optimized sparse matmuls where available. For Llama-derived models you'll want to enable rotary embeddings and our runtime's fused rotary kernels for speed.
10:20 Rae Martin: On the earlier point about global summary vectors — will that bias generation? We worry it might lead the model down a single interpretation path.
10:33 Ethan Park: Good flag. The summary vectors are used as a soft signal for retrieval and scoring but not as a hard constraint on generation. We tune mixture weights and provide feedback loops to detect mode collapse. If you prefer we can run an ablation in the pilot to check for drift.
10:55 Maya Chen: Ok there's a lot here. Let's walk through a potential pilot plan.
11:00 Ethan Park: Pilot plan idea: 1) You hand over a representative subset (5–10k requests, including 128k initial conditions). 2) Redwood runs two configs: full-GPU-resident KV and hybrid NVMe-prefetch. 3) We'll run perf tests under your bursty concurrency and collect p50/p95/p99 latencies and cost per 1k output tokens. 4) We'll also provide calibrated quantization map and evaluate accuracy regression.
11:34 Amina Farouk: That sounds reasonable. Need to make sure the perf data excludes PII exposure. We'll scrub and provide redaction rules.
11:45 Priya Narang: We'll accept scrubbed data; if you prefer we can also execute the pilot in your VPC via Private deployment so no data exits your network.
12:00 Lucas Romero: If we go Private pilot, do you need any special infra from our side?
12:10 Priya Narang: We'll need access to a bastion host and a route for the control plane (or we can do an air-gapped control plane for sensitive setups). Also the standard images, storage endpoints, and KMS endpoints. We'll share a deployment checklist.
12:30 Samir Patel: Regarding compliance, do you provide SOC2 reports and a data processing addendum?
12:38 Maya Chen: Yes, we'll hand over SOC2 attestation and a DPA. For Private deployments we can add stricter contractual language.
12:50 Rae Martin: A specific technical question: when doing mixed quantization, do you see gradient-quality like issues for logits in extraction tasks?
12:58 Ethan Park: For inference-only quant we don't do gradients, but calibration can distort logits slightly. We mitigate by keeping final softmax layers higher precision and by using bias correction in quant tables. In our pharma tests we usually see <0.5% F1 drop with careful calibration using holdout tokens.
13:25 Lucas Romero: Any known gotchas for NVMe sharding on GCP? We run local SSDs but network-attached NVMe is slower.
13:36 Priya Narang: We recommend local NVMe where possible, with a fallback to networked if local is constrained. Also watch for GCE ephemeral disk preemption and design for checkpointing KV metadata.
13:55 Jenna Park: On cost — can Redwood show an estimate for our projected 1M requests/month with average 3k output tokens?
14:05 Maya Chen: Yes, that's one of the next steps — we'll model cost under both Dedicated and Private modes. That will include GPU-hour estimates, NVMe costs, and caching delta.
14:20 Amina Farouk: Any open-source connectors you provide, or is everything bespoke?
14:27 Ethan Park: We provide a perf harness repo, calibration scripts, and an agent that can run in your infra to collect telemetry. The runtime is closed-source but we have SDKs and agents.
14:40 Lucas Romero: For rollout, can you do canary on per-team basis so some requests go to a cheaper quantized variant?
14:49 Ethan Park: Yes — our rollout supports traffic splitting by model version and by per-route policies, including automatic fallback if the quantized variant regresses on eval prompts.
15:05 Jenna Park: What's the expected timeline for a pilot? From signature to first perf run?
15:12 Maya Chen: Typically 2–3 weeks if dataset and infra access are available. Private deployment adds setup time — 1–2 additional weeks.
15:25 Samir Patel: For KMS, we need HSM-backed keys and CMEK integration. Is customer-managed HSM supported?
15:34 Priya Narang: We support integrating with customer-managed KMS and HSM providers; we'll need a short technical checklist of endpoints and permissions.
15:50 Rae Martin: Any notes on model warmup? For 128k context we assume warmup time to populate KV.
15:58 Ethan Park: Yes, warmup is crucial. We run a background warmup process that preloads KV shards based on your access patterns; we can also snapshot warmed state to reduce cold start. Warmed snapshot restore takes minutes depending on KV size.
16:25 Lucas Romero: One more: how do you measure correctness/regression after quantization?
16:33 Ethan Park: We'll run your eval prompts and compute task-specific metrics (F1, exact match, hallucination indicators). We also provide a prompt-level diff tool to surface where outputs diverge. If the quantized model regresses, rollout rules can route a small percent to a higher-precision fallback.
16:55 Maya Chen: Ok let's recap and surface action items.
17:00 Maya Chen: Action items: Maya send perf harness and cost sheet; Lucas provide dataset and infra constraints; Priya draft Private deploy network and KMS doc; Rae provide chunking examples and key prompts; Redwood to propose pilot schedule week of Oct 18th.
17:20 Amina Farouk: Thanks — please include the calibration scripts and recommended quant profiles so our team can prep.
17:30 Maya Chen: We'll include it. Any final quick questions?
17:40 Jenna Park: Nothing more, thanks everyone.
17:45 Ethan Park: Thanks all — we'll follow up with links and the next calendar invite.

(End of transcript)
